nameStory: The red-headed bush cricket gets its name from the distinctive reddish-orange coloring on its head, which makes it stand out from other small crickets. It's also called the 'handsome trig' because of its attractive appearance and membership in the trig cricket family - 'trig' being short for Trigonidiidae, named for their triangular face shape.
description: The red-headed bush cricket is a small, delicate cricket about the size of your pinky nail. It has a striking reddish-orange head that contrasts beautifully with its pale green to brownish body. Unlike the chunky field crickets you might know, this little cricket has a more slender build and spends its time climbing around on low vegetation rather than hopping on the ground.

idTips.label: Reddish-orange head
idTips.description: The head glows with a warm orange-red color that's unmistakable once you spot it - like a tiny ember among the green leaves

idTips.label: Small, delicate size
idTips.description: Only about 3-4mm long, roughly the size of a ladybug, with thin legs and antennae that give it a fragile appearance

idTips.label: Pale body coloration
idTips.description: Body ranges from pale green to light brown, often with a translucent quality that makes it blend into plant stems

idTips.label: Active climber
idTips.description: Moves deliberately up and down plant stems rather than making sudden jumps, often pausing motionless when disturbed

idTips.label: Clear wing covers
idTips.description: Wings appear almost glassy or transparent with delicate veining visible, quite different from the opaque wings of larger crickets

habitat: Look for red-headed bush crickets in weedy fields, forest edges, and gardens where they climb on low shrubs, tall grasses, and herbaceous plants. They prefer areas with mixed vegetation rather than dense forests, often found on goldenrod, asters, and other wildflowers in late summer.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; overwintering eggs are developing in plant stems and soil.
seasonality.summer: Young nymphs begin appearing in mid to late summer, climbing on low vegetation but without the full adult coloration.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity time when fully mature adults with bright red-orange heads are most visible and males produce their soft chirping songs.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with first hard frost; eggs overwinter in plant material and will hatch the following summer.

funFact: Despite being called a 'bush cricket,' these tiny musicians actually produce their songs by rubbing their wings together so gently that their chirps are nearly inaudible to human ears - you'd need to put your ear within inches of one to hear its whisper-soft serenade!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small green crickets and katydids, but the bright orange-red head is a dead giveaway - no other small cricket in New England sports such vibrant head coloring. Remember: red head, right ID!
contextualKnowledge: The name 'trig' cricket comes from the family name Trigonidiidae, referring to their somewhat triangular face shape when viewed head-on. Don't confuse these delicate bush-dwelling species with the robust ground crickets that live in leaf litter.
compareHints: As the only Phyllopalpus species in New England, the red-headed bush cricket is unique in its genus here. Among other trig crickets in the region, it's distinguished by its prominent red-orange head coloration and preference for climbing on vegetation rather than living in leaf litter like many of its ground-dwelling relatives.
